definition: A short, sturdy vertical post, sometimes retractable, placed outside a building or walkway to stop vehicles from getting close.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 43: Physical Security

definition: A small entry space between two interlocking doors where a person is held until identified, which stops tailgating.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 43: Physical Security

definition: A device beside a door that reads an employee's photo ID or proximity card, often by RFID, and unlocks the door for authorized holders.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 43: Physical Security

definition: A system of door and window sensors and motion detectors that sounds a siren and alerts a central monitoring service when someone breaks in.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 43: Physical Security

definition: A detector, usually infrared (heat) or ultrasonic, that notices movement in a protected area and triggers an alarm or turns on lights.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 43: Physical Security

definition: A walk-through scanner at an entry point that uses an electromagnetic field to find concealed metal weapons or equipment being carried out.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 5: Security Concepts

definition: Bright illumination of a building's perimeter and entrances that deters intruders, removes hiding places, and lets security cameras record clear images.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 43: Physical Security

definition: A small proximity token on a keychain that a user holds near a reader to unlock a door, like a smaller version of an entry card.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 43: Physical Security

definition: A credential card with an embedded chip that talks to the authentication system and can also sign and encrypt data, such as a PIV or CAC card.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 43: Physical Security

definition: A secure credential stored on a phone that unlocks doors or cars over NFC or Bluetooth and can be revoked remotely if the phone is lost.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 43: Physical Security

definition: A biometric reader that shines low-energy infrared light into the eye to map the unique pattern of blood vessels at the back of it.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 5: Security Concepts

definition: A biometric reader that captures the ridges, lines, and creases across a person's whole hand, a larger area than a single fingertip.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 5: Security Concepts

definition: A biometric method that identifies a person by analyzing the pitch, tone, and cadence of their speech to build a voiceprint.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 43: Physical Security

definition: The rule that each user or program gets only the access and rights needed to do its job, and no more.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 44: Logical Security

definition: A security approach of never trust, always verify, which requires authentication and authorization for every request, even from inside the network perimeter.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 44: Logical Security

definition: A list of entries attached to an object or firewall that states which users, groups, addresses, or ports are allowed or denied.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 44: Logical Security

definition: Granting elevated rights only at the moment they are needed and removing them automatically when the task ends, as with sudo in Linux.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 44: Logical Security

definition: A strategy and toolset that vaults admin credentials, records admin sessions, and grants elevated rights only temporarily to protect high-power accounts.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 44: Logical Security

definition: Tools that watch data in use and in transit and block sensitive information, such as customer records, from being emailed or copied outside the organization.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 44: Logical Security

definition: The policies and systems that verify who each user is and control what each one may reach, including provisioning, deprovisioning, and auditing accounts.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 44: Logical Security

definition: An authentication arrangement in which one login with one set of credentials gives a user access to many applications and systems.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 44: Logical Security

definition: An XML-based open standard that passes authentication and authorization data from an identity provider to a service provider, making web single sign-on possible.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 44: Logical Security

definition: Logging in with two or more different kinds of proof, such as something you know, something you have, and something you are.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 44: Logical Security

definition: A small physical device, such as an RSA key fob, that generates one-time passcodes; it is hard to copy unless stolen.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 44: Logical Security

definition: A phone app, such as Google Authenticator, that generates time-based codes for a second login step without relying on text messages.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 44: Logical Security

definition: A short code calculated from a shared secret and the current time that changes every 30 seconds or so, and needs synchronized clocks.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 44: Logical Security

definition: A single-use code, delivered by text, email, voice call, app, or hardware token, that is invalid after one login, which defeats replay attacks.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 44: Logical Security

definition: A Windows user account that exists only on one computer, needs no email address, and does not sync settings to other devices.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: A Windows sign-in tied to an email address and online profile that syncs settings, OneDrive files, and Store apps across devices.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: The default Windows account level, which can use apps and its own data but cannot install software or change system settings without elevation.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: The most powerful Windows account level, with full control of the computer, including installing software and managing other users.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: A built-in, disabled-by-default Windows account with very limited temporary access that cannot install software, change settings, or change its password.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: The Windows feature that runs users with standard rights and shows a consent or credential prompt before any task that needs administrative rights.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 44: Logical Security

definition: The built-in Windows antimalware tool, found under Virus & threat protection, that runs scans, updates definitions, and can have real-time protection turned off.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: The built-in Windows host firewall, opened with firewall.cpl or wf.msc, that blocks unsolicited inbound traffic per network profile and allows app or port exceptions.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: The Windows passwordless sign-in feature that uses a face scan, a fingerprint, or a PIN tied to that one device, with data kept in the TPM.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: The Windows Pro and Enterprise feature that encrypts a whole internal drive with AES, using a TPM chip or a USB key to hold the keys.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: The Windows feature that applies full-drive encryption to USB flash drives and other removable media, protected by a password or smart card.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: The NTFS feature that encrypts individual files and folders for one user through the Advanced Attributes checkbox; it does not encrypt whole drives.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: Encrypting information while it sits on a storage device, such as a drive or tape, so it stays unreadable if the device is stolen.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 48: Workstation Best Practices

definition: Permissions set on the Security tab that apply to a file or folder both locally and over the network, from Read up to Full Control.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: Permissions set on the Sharing tab, Read, Change, or Full Control, that apply only when a folder is reached over the network.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: The default behavior in which a new subfolder or file takes on the permissions of its parent folder until this is disabled.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: A concealed share, such as C$ or ADMIN$, that Windows creates automatically for administrators and that ends with a dollar sign.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: Microsoft's directory service, run on Windows Server domain controllers, that centrally manages user accounts, computers, and policies for a domain.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: A container in Active Directory used to sort users and computers, often by department, so each set can get its own Group Policy.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: The Windows rule system, edited with gpedit.msc locally or GPOs in a domain and refreshed with gpupdate, that controls user and computer settings.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: A batch or PowerShell file that runs automatically when a user signs in to a domain to map drives, set printers, or start programs.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: Sending a user's Documents or Desktop folder to a network share instead of the local drive, so files follow the user to any computer.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: An Active Directory group, such as Domain Admins or Backup Operators, used to assign permissions and access to many users at once.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 45: Windows Security Settings

definition: The wireless security standard, also called 802.11i, that uses AES with CCMP and offers Personal (pre-shared key) and Enterprise (RADIUS) modes.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 6: Securing Operating Systems

definition: The newest wireless security standard, required for certification since 2020, with stronger key exchange than its predecessor and 192-bit strength in Enterprise mode.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 6: Securing Operating Systems

definition: An older wireless encryption method from the original WPA that wraps the RC4 cipher with per-packet keys; it is deprecated and weaker than AES.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 6: Securing Operating Systems

definition: A strong symmetric block cipher with 128- or 256-bit keys, used by WPA2, WPA3, BitLocker, and EFS.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 46: Wireless Security and Malware

definition: A central AAA server for VPN, dial-up, and enterprise Wi-Fi logons that uses UDP ports 1812 and 1813 and combines authentication with authorization.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 46: Wireless Security and Malware

term: Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus
definition: A Cisco-developed AAA protocol that uses TCP port 49 and keeps authentication, authorization, and accounting as separate steps.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 46: Wireless Security and Malware

definition: A ticket-based authentication protocol on port 88 that provides mutual authentication when users log on to an Active Directory domain controller.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 46: Wireless Security and Malware

definition: Malicious code that attaches to a host file or program and spreads when that file is run or shared, often damaging files.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 5: Security Concepts

definition: Malware disguised as a useful or legitimate program that the user installs willingly, which then opens a backdoor or delivers other malware.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 46: Wireless Security and Malware

definition: Malware that gains administrator-level control and hides itself inside the operating system, so it is usually found only by scanning from outside the OS.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 46: Wireless Security and Malware

definition: Malware that infects the master boot record or boot sector, so it loads before the operating system; Secure Boot helps block it.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 5: Security Concepts

definition: Malicious code that runs in memory through trusted tools like PowerShell instead of executable files on disk, making it hard to detect.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 5: Security Concepts

definition: Malware that encrypts a victim's files or locks the system and demands payment, usually in cryptocurrency, for the decryption key.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 5: Security Concepts

definition: Malware, often JavaScript on a malicious web page, that secretly uses a victim's CPU or GPU to mine cryptocurrency, causing slowdowns and high usage.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 5: Security Concepts

definition: Malware that secretly gathers information about a user's activity, such as browsing habits or personal data, and sends it to a third party.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 46: Wireless Security and Malware

definition: Software or a small hardware device that records every keystroke to capture passwords and other typed data.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 5: Security Concepts

definition: Monitoring software, secretly installed on one person's phone by someone they know, that reveals messages, calls, and location to that other person.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 5: Security Concepts

definition: Software that shows unwanted advertisements, such as pop-ups and banners, to earn money for its maker, often slowing the device.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 5: Security Concepts

definition: Software, often bundled with a legitimate download, that the user did not mean to install, such as toolbars or ad add-ons.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 5: Security Concepts

definition: A set of repair tools that runs outside normal Windows, in Windows called WinRE, offering Startup Repair, System Restore, Command Prompt, and image recovery.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 46: Wireless Security and Malware

definition: An agent on each computer that continuously records process, network, and file activity to detect suspicious behavior and help respond to it.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 46: Wireless Security and Malware

definition: An outsourced service in which a provider's analysts monitor an organization's security tools around the clock and hunt for and respond to threats.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 5: Security Concepts

definition: A platform that collects and correlates security data from endpoints, networks, servers, email, and cloud, not just from endpoints.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 46: Wireless Security and Malware

definition: Security software that mainly compares files against a database of known signatures, so its definitions must be kept up to date.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 46: Wireless Security and Malware

definition: Security software that adds heuristic and behavior analysis to signature matching, so it can catch spyware, rootkits, and new threats as well.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 46: Wireless Security and Malware

definition: The malware removal step of isolating an infected computer from the network and shared drives so the infection cannot spread.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security

definition: A Windows startup option that loads only basic drivers and services, which limits malware activity while a scan runs.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security

definition: A small bootable operating system, such as Windows PE on a USB drive, used to scan and repair a computer from outside its installed OS.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security

definition: The last-resort removal step of wiping the drive and restoring a clean standard image or reinstalling the OS, after backing up the user's data.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security

definition: A saved snapshot of Windows system files and settings; after malware is removed, System Restore is turned back on and a new one is made.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security

definition: A fraudulent email or website that pretends to come from a trusted organization to trick many people into giving up credentials or personal information.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: Voice-based fraud in which a phone call, often an automated VoIP message, pretends to be a bank or company to get account details.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: Fraud carried out with text messages, such as a fake delivery or tax notice, that urges the recipient to tap a malicious link.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: A scam that uses a fake scannable code, for example a sticker over a parking meter's real one, to send victims to a credential-stealing site.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: A fraudulent message campaign tailored to a specific group or person using researched details, rather than sent to thousands of random people.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: A targeted fraud campaign aimed at senior executives, the high-value targets of an organization.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: A scam in which attackers pose as an executive or vendor in email to trick employees into wiring money or sending sensitive data.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: Manipulating people, rather than systems, into revealing confidential information or performing actions that harm security.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: Watching someone directly, or with a camera, as they type a password or PIN; a privacy filter helps prevent it.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: Following an authorized person through a secured door without their knowledge or consent; an access control vestibule prevents it.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: Pretending to be another person, such as a technician, vendor, or manager, often with a made-up story, to gain access or information.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: Searching through trash and recycling bins for documents, drives, or notes that contain sensitive information; shredding prevents it.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: An attack from one source, such as a ping or SYN flood, that overwhelms a server or network so legitimate users cannot reach it.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: An attack in which many compromised computers in a botnet flood one target at the same time to make it unavailable.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: A rogue wireless access point that uses the same SSID as a legitimate nearby network to lure users and capture their traffic.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: An exploit of a software flaw that the vendor does not yet know about or has not patched, so no fix exists when it is used.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: Falsifying identifying information, such as an IP address, MAC address, or email sender, to masquerade as a trusted source.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: An attack in which the attacker secretly sits between two communicating hosts to intercept, read, or alter their traffic; formerly called man-in-the-middle.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: Cracking a password by trying every possible combination of characters; it always works eventually but takes long against lengthy passwords.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: Cracking a password by trying words from a prepared list of likely words and common passwords, one after another.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: An attack that types database commands into a poorly validated web form so the database reveals or changes data; input validation prevents it.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: An attack that plants malicious script, often JavaScript, in a trusted web page so it runs in visitors' browsers and steals cookies or session data.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: Danger from an employee, contractor, or planted device already inside the organization, whether the harm is deliberate or accidental.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: Compromising a trusted third-party product, service, or software delivery pipeline in order to reach the organizations that use it.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: A computer that breaks the organization's security policy, for example by missing required updates or antimalware, and so weakens the whole network.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

definition: A computer running without antivirus software or a firewall, leaving it open to malware and network attacks.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 5: Security Concepts

definition: A rule that a password must mix character types, in Windows at least three of uppercase, lowercase, digits, and special characters.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 48: Workstation Best Practices

definition: A policy that forces a password change after a set time, such as the Windows default of 42 days; NIST now advises it only after a breach.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 48: Workstation Best Practices

definition: A Windows policy that remembers a user's previous passwords so they cannot be reused when the password is changed.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 48: Workstation Best Practices

definition: An application or browser feature that stores credentials in an encrypted vault and can generate long, unique passwords for every site.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 48: Workstation Best Practices

definition: A policy that locks a user account after a set number of failed logon attempts, which slows password-guessing attacks.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 48: Workstation Best Practices

definition: An account setting that allows a user to sign in only during chosen hours and days, such as weekdays from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 48: Workstation Best Practices

definition: A password-protected screensaver or timeout that locks an idle computer, so the user must sign in again when returning.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 48: Workstation Best Practices

definition: The Windows feature that automatically starts a program from inserted removable media; turning it off stops embedded malware from launching.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 48: Workstation Best Practices

definition: Any data that can identify a specific person, such as a name with a birth date, an ID number, or an address, which must be protected.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 48: Workstation Best Practices

definition: A phone or tablet setting that requires a face, fingerprint, PIN, pattern, or password before the device can be used after a timeout.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 49: Mobile Device Security

definition: A set of security settings, often pushed by MDM, that enforces policies on mobile devices, such as password rules, app limits, and VPN setup.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 49: Mobile Device Security

definition: Keeping operating systems and applications current by finding, testing, and installing updates that fix security flaws.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 49: Mobile Device Security

definition: Antivirus, anti-malware, firewall, and content filtering apps installed on a phone or tablet to protect it from threats.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 49: Mobile Device Security

definition: An app, such as Find My or Find My Device, that uses GPS to show where a lost or stolen phone is.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 49: Mobile Device Security

definition: A command sent over the internet to a lost or stolen mobile device that erases all of its data.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 49: Mobile Device Security

definition: Physically destroying a hard drive by boring holes through its platters so it cannot be read.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 50: Data Destruction and Disposal

definition: Feeding storage drives into an industrial machine that tears them into small pieces, also called pulverizing, usually done by a third-party vendor.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 50: Data Destruction and Disposal

definition: Erasing magnetic media with a strong electromagnetic field, which also leaves a hard drive unusable; it does not work on SSDs.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 50: Data Destruction and Disposal

definition: Destroying storage media or documents by burning them completely, usually at a licensed facility.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 50: Data Destruction and Disposal

definition: Overwriting every sector of a drive with zeros or patterns, for example with format /p or diskpart clean all, so the drive can be reused.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 50: Data Destruction and Disposal

definition: A physical format, done by the manufacturer, that creates the tracks and sectors on a hard disk; users rely on zero-fill tools instead.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 50: Data Destruction and Disposal

definition: A format done from the OS that writes a new file system; quick mode only removes access to files, while full mode also zeros the partition.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 50: Data Destruction and Disposal

definition: A document from a third-party vendor that proves storage media were destroyed or recycled, often required by data privacy laws.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 50: Data Destruction and Disposal

definition: A router setting that allows or blocks devices according to a list of addresses entered in advance.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security

definition: Blocking websites or content by category, domain, or schedule, as with a router's family safety page or a mobile security app.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security

definition: A set of protocols that lets devices discover each other and open router ports automatically; it is often disabled because malware can abuse it.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security

definition: A network segment between the internet and the LAN, protected by a firewall, for servers the public must reach; formerly called a DMZ.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security

definition: A router rule that sends traffic arriving on an external port to a chosen internal IP address and port, such as a web server.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security

definition: The factory-set credential, often blank or admin, that must be changed first when setting up a router, before anything else.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security

definition: A router setting that requires an encrypted protocol, such as HTTPS, for the admin login so credentials are not sent in plaintext.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security

definition: The name of a wireless network; its default value should be changed, and its broadcast can be turned off to hide it from casual scans.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security

definition: A separate wireless network that gives visitors or IoT devices internet access but keeps them away from internal resources and main-network clients.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security

definition: A push-button or 8-digit PIN method for joining wireless devices easily; it should be disabled because the PIN is open to brute-force attacks.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security

definition: A known, legitimate provider of downloads, such as the vendor's own site or official extension store, approved by the organization's policy.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 52: Browser Security

definition: A download site, forum, or third-party store that is unknown or unreliable, so files from it may be altered or contain malware.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 52: Browser Security

definition: Running a file through a one-way algorithm to produce a fixed-length value that, compared with the publisher's value, proves the download was not altered.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 52: Browser Security

definition: A small add-on program, installed from a store such as the Chrome Web Store, that adds features to a web browser and can be enabled or disabled.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 52: Browser Security

definition: An older type of browser add-on that handles specific content, such as a video codec or decryption module, now mostly replaced by extensions.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 52: Browser Security

definition: An electronic credential, issued by a trusted authority, that proves a website's identity and enables HTTPS; the browser warns when it is expired or invalid.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 52: Browser Security

definition: A browser setting that stops sites from opening new windows on their own, which blocks many ads and scam prompts.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 6: Securing Operating Systems

definition: Deleting a browser's stored history, cookies, saved form entries, and passwords so other users of the computer cannot see them.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 6: Securing Operating Systems

definition: Deleting the browser's locally stored copies of web pages and images, which fixes pages that show outdated content or load incorrectly.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 6: Securing Operating Systems

definition: A browser window, InPrivate in Edge or Incognito in Chrome (Ctrl+Shift+N), that keeps no history, cookies, or cache after it closes.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 52: Browser Security

definition: Signing in to a browser account so bookmarks, history, passwords, and settings are copied to every device that uses the same account.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 6: Securing Operating Systems

definition: A browser extension or setting that stops advertisements from loading, which also limits tracking and adware.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 52: Browser Security

definition: Encrypting name-lookup requests, for example with DNS over HTTPS, so third parties cannot read or tamper with them.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 52: Browser Security
